Start Here

Welcome to After the Storm.

I'm Jennifer — a single mom of six, a college student, and a survivor. This is where I'm telling the truth about the trauma that ran throughout my life: what it cost, what it taught me, and what healing actually looks like.

You'll find the hard parts here — my childhood, the years in survival mode, the men I picked wrong, and becoming the mom I wished I'd had. And you'll find the healing parts too, as I get to them. I'm telling it in my own words, one honest post at a time.

If any of this sounds like your life, you're in the right place. Subscribe for free and new posts will land in your inbox as I write them — and if something I wrote speaks to you, tell me in the comments. I'd love to hear it.

By Jennifer · November 12, 2026

Childhood Abuse

As long as I can remember, I don't remember a time when I wasn't being sexually abused.

It taught me that I had to do things for people to care about me — exactly the wrong definition of unconditional love.

Thank you for reading the start of my story. There's more to come, one piece at a time.
— Jennifer

By Jennifer · November 12, 2026

Why Was I Chosen for This Life?

There are so many moments that go through my mind, making me wonder: why was I chosen for this life?

Many people would say things to me as a young child — that I was a brat, and selfish, and whined. Those words became my inner voice.

I was just simply a child dealing with such immense trauma. I had no idea how to behave, or how to let all those emotions out, other than acting out. I guess, looking back, I realize now that I was screaming for love. Not the conditional love — for someone to just give me attention, and choose me, and show me the real meaning of love.

Back then, you didn't talk about abuse. Family got away with it because they were family. So do I speak up, or stay quiet to protect the family — the only "family" I ever knew? So many things that a young child should never have to wonder about.

By Jennifer · November 12, 2026

Outside the Circle

The Ones Who Loved Me

I don't have many memories as a child. I guess my brain is protecting me. I do remember a lot of the abuse, but some of my fondest memories were spending time with my grandpa. We would mow the lawn together, and every Saturday we would go to the dump, and then on the way home stop and get me a candy bar. He always watched Hee Haw with me!

My Gramma Pat used to take me to work with her in the mornings before school, and I loved helping her at the diner. She definitely spoiled me. She was a very amazing woman, and the only one in my childhood who seemed to love me as me. She was a very stoic person, though, and you never really heard or felt her love — you just knew she loved you by the way she was. I lost her in 2005, and that moment changed me forever. I felt I had lost the only person that had ever just loved me unconditionally and without limits.

Survival Mode

When a child is abused, I feel like they stop growing emotionally, and it puts them into a state of survival mode. I now know that I spent many years in that mode, not really knowing what I was doing. I know in my early teens and young adult life I had so much anger, and I have never had a filter or patience, and it showed during those early adult years. Those qualities sometimes served me well, especially when I needed to advocate for my children. I became the protector of children that I wished I had as a little girl. No one really protected me, or took the time to understand how I was feeling, or made sure I was mentally and emotionally okay.

On the Sidelines

I remember always, at family gatherings and events, I felt like I was sitting outside the circle looking in. Even as a kid with friends, I was never the chosen kid. I was always on the sidelines trying to do my best to be liked, but somehow that skill evaded me as a child. I remember thinking, all I want to be is a wife and a mom, so my children will have that picture-perfect childhood I always yearned for — and I definitely tried my best to give my children that. But we will talk more about that in another writing. I don't want to get ahead of myself.

What I Learned About Love

I learned that people only love you when they have something to gain by loving you or from you. That reality hit me when I was about 13, and it was such a revelation — you would think it would have helped me to gain some insight on how to love. Nope, it didn't. I began to seek attention from men, and lots of men. What a horrific decision that was.

About Jennifer

Jennifer is a mom of six and a college student in New York. Her days are full — family, work, and classes — and this blog is where her story gets told alongside all of it, in her own words and at her own pace.

She started After the Storm for two reasons: because stories of living through trauma shouldn't have to stay locked away, and because she hopes the writing will reach — and one day help support — the people who find it.

What you'll find here: her posts as she writes them. Nothing posted in her name that she didn't write or approve.

  • Mom of six
  • College student

  • Favorite color: blue

How this blog grows

After the Storm was started with two hopes: that these stories reach the people who need them, and that in time the writing itself could earn something back. Honest blogs grow the slow way — one true post and one reader at a time. Here's the road:

1Stories first

New posts, added as Jennifer writes them. Consistency and honesty are what bring readers back.

2Readers who stay

As the audience grows, the next step is a simple email list so readers never miss a post — the foundation every earning blog is built on.

3From readers to income

With steady readers come the real options: reader support, partnerships with brands that fit this space, and one day, gathering these stories into a book.

The simplest way to help right now:

If you're in a hard moment

Jennifer is a writer sharing her own story — not a therapist, and this blog is not medical advice. If what you're carrying feels like too much right now, please reach out to people trained to help. In the US:

988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

Call or text 988

Free, confidential support, 24/7, anywhere in the United States.

988lifeline.org

Crisis Text Line

Text HOME to 741741

Connect with a live, trained counselor by text, 24/7.

crisistextline.org

SAMHSA Helpline

1-800-662-4357

Free referrals and information for mental health and substance-use support, 24/7.

samhsa.gov
